title: Origins of the bands: European and African elements, rhythm
summary: Russell discusses theories of origin, African versus European influence, and the swing and beat at the heart of the music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, these bands that started here in New Orleans, how did they start?

Well, there's a lot of theories on it that came from the parade music and came from blues or from some of the work songs. Actually, a lot of it is European. And there's this big argument about the African influence on it, which is difficult to prove. There was definitely an African strain in it, though, as far as I've been able to discover, too. Certain elements there that I've never come across in ordinary European music.
Well, the rhythm is so much stronger than European music, isn't it?

Maybe, but not necessarily. There have been some strong, like, look at the Spanish music. Yeah. And some of that was influenced by African music, too. Well, this also... The Cuban type of music. It's all very rhythmic.
Well, this rhythmic element is basic to what we now call jazz, though, isn't it?

Oh, yes. It's one of the main things, is the definite rhythm to it, the definite beat that it has, and a certain kind of, not necessarily just simple syncopation, as they usually used to talk about, but there's just a certain kind of a swing to it. They never have found really a good term to express it, but once you hear it, I mean, you get that feeling, a foot-tapping feeling, and a certain happy feeling about the beat that goes on and on.
